title: Are Sustainable and Healthy Eating Behaviors and Levels of Nutritional Knowledge Associated with Obesity and Chronic Disease Risk Among Healthcare Workers?
content: Objectives: This study evaluated the relationship between sustainable and healthy eating behaviors and nutritional knowledge with obesity and chronic disease risk determined by anthropometric indicators among healthcare workers. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 1,070 healthcare workers aged 22–59 years in Isparta, Türkiye. Data were collected face-to-face using a questionnaire including sociodemographic characteristics, the Sustainable and Healthy Eating Behaviors Scale (SHE), and the Nutrition Knowledge Level Scale for Adults (NKLSA). Anthropometric measurements included body weight, height, waist, hip and neck circumferences, waist-to-hip ratio, and waist-to-height ratio. Obesity was classified by body mass index, and chronic disease risk was evaluated using established cut-off points. Chi-square test, Student’s t-test, one-way ANOVA, correlation analysis, and structural equation modeling were used. Results: 27.9% of participants were overweight and 27.1% had obesity. Chronic disease risk was identified in 55.8% by waist circumference, 54.8% by neck circumference, 55.0% by waist-to-hip ratio, and 50.0% by waist-to-height ratio. The mean SHE score was 126.53 ± 61.65. SHE scores decreased with increasing BMI and were lower among at-risk participants based on waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio. Nutritional knowledge was strongly correlated with SHE, whereas SHE was negatively correlated with BMI, waist circumference, and waist-to-hip ratio. Mediation analysis showed that SHE mediated the relationship between nutritional knowledge and anthropometric indicators, except neck circumference. Conclusions: Overweight, obesity, chronic disease risk were common among healthcare workers. Higher nutritional knowledge was associated with better sustainable and healthy eating behaviors and lower obesity risk. Workplace nutrition education may translate knowledge into healthy dietary behaviors.
